items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman (David Curtin note)
items.title: Goldman: higher yields are cracking two unrelated borrowers — French sovereign debt and AI infrastructure financing
items.idea: Goldman rates strategist David Curtin flags early strain among borrowers with large existing debt AND large future financing needs. The two places it shows up: French sovereigns and the AI buildout financing stack. The AI debate is shifting from compute demand and earnings to a financing constraint that may set the pace of capex, with an unusual cross-asset reversal between AI capex and long-bond yields taking shape.
items.angle: The same bid-less duration buyer funds OATs and data-center paper. Watch whether $ORCL/$CRWV spreads and OAT-Bund move together.
items.tweetA: France and CoreWeave have the same problem: big stock of debt, bigger need to roll it, and a marginal buyer who just got repriced. Different logos, one balance sheet shape. $CRWV $ORCL
items.tweetB: For two years capex pushed yields up. Now yields may be the thing that caps capex. If that loop closes, the AI trade has a governor it never priced.

items.source: The Dark Side of the Boom / Goldman (Brian Garrett, Peter Callahan)
items.title: Goldman: hedge funds hedged a lot but still carry a lot — record downside protection changes market structure
items.idea: Per Goldman prime/derivatives work (via Dark Side of the Boom), there is a disconnect between how much risk funds have hedged and how much remains on the books. A record rush into downside protection reshaped near-term structure, while credit and single-stock vol signals say the adjustment is more complicated than the index implies. Earnings season is framed as the test of whether investors rebuild positions.
items.angle: Record put demand plus Black Monday headlines is the setup where dealers end up long gamma into the print. Fade the crash narrative, respect the gap risk.
items.tweetA: Everyone bought protection on the way down. Nobody has said what they do with it if earnings are fine. Hedges are a bid for stocks the moment they get monetized.
items.tweetB: Gross exposure barely moved while hedge ratios jumped. That's not de-risking, that's insurance on a house you still own. Different thing when the fire doesn't come.

items.title: Understanding the bond sell-off: Homer's 5,000 years of rates say post-2008 was the anomaly
items.idea: Sidney Homer's A History of Interest Rates (1963) spans five millennia; the lesson is that ultra-low and negative post-GFC yields were historically unique. The author builds a hybrid Anglo-American long-term yield from US Treasury and Bank of England archives and argues 'normal' rates are returning. US 10s are far above COVID sub-1%, and the open question is whether bonds are finally worth owning.
items.angle: This is the long-history frame for the 10y breakout Hi Mount and Boockvar flag in the same window. Term premium as regime, not shock.
items.tweetA: The 10y isn't spiking, it's mean-reverting to a 5,000-year average. The anomaly was 2009–2021. Your duration models were calibrated on the anomaly.
items.tweetB: After a 12-year financial repression window, 'bonds offer income again' is the least surprising sentence in macro. The surprising part is how many balance sheets were built on the opposite assumption.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider (WarTalk w/ Travis Metz)
items.title: Pentagon's Drone Dominance: $1.1B, 209 submissions to 30,000 drones in ~5 months
items.idea: DIU's Travis Metz: reconciliation money ($1.1B) used to simply place orders in a six-month 'Gauntlet' cycle. Timeline: announced Nov, RFP Dec, 209 submissions Jan, 25 invited to Fort Benning Feb, orders March. First round was 30,000 mostly unweaponized one-way attack quadcopters (15 km range). Weaponized units priced about $5,000 in the first batch and $4,000 in the second, versus $500–2,000 in Ukraine.
items.angle: Procurement-by-purchase-order is the template. Price per unit falling ~20% per cycle is the number to track across defense tech names.
items.tweetA: $5,000 to $4,000 in one six-month cycle just from competition. That's a Wright's-law curve on a weapon system, run by the Pentagon. Defense primes should read this nervously.
items.tweetB: 209 submissions to 25 finalists to orders in 3 months. The DoD that took 7 years to field a rifle just ran a reverse auction. Whoever wins the supply chain owns the next decade of munitions.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider (WarTalk w/ Travis Metz)
items.title: 8 million quadcopters on the Ukrainian side this year; 70–80% of recent casualties from drones
items.idea: Metz estimates ~8 million quads used on the Ukrainian side this year, and says depending on data source 70–80% of casualties in recent months come from these systems and octocopter bombers. He also notes US doctrine will differ (higher altitudes, different adversary) and that short-range quads are 'probably not the fulcrum issue' for US problem sets.
items.angle: At $500–2,000 a unit, 8M quads is a $4–16B annual market on one side of one war. Munitions demand is a consumer-electronics supply chain problem now.
items.tweetA: 8M drones a year. At Ukrainian prices that's $4–16B on one side of one front, spent on things that fit in a backpack. The artillery shell stocks everyone trades are the old war.
items.tweetB: 70–80% of casualties from a $1,000 object. Every tank, every APC, every defense budget line is being re-priced against that fact.

items.source: ChinaTalk / Jordan Schneider (WarTalk w/ Travis Metz)
items.title: US drone industry is 'wide but not deep': Chinese motor and battery bans collide with rare-earth and cell-chemistry dependence
items.idea: First Drone Dominance orders ban Chinese motors and battery packs, testing how far supply-chain decoupling can go. Metz says the program can't by itself solve dependencies in battery chemistry and rare-earth refining. Policy rule: sellers must be on a journey to being US manufacturers, which makes it hard for battle-tested Ukrainian firms to compete.
items.angle: Same chokepoints as every other 'onshoring' story: magnets and cells. Drone orders are a clean demand signal for non-China motors and batteries.
items.tweetA: You can ban the motor. You can't ban the neodymium that's in it. Decoupling stops at refining, and refining is where China has the whole stack.
items.tweetB: The Pentagon just created a guaranteed buyer for non-Chinese small motors and cells. That's a cleaner demand signal than any ESG fund flow.

items.source: The Daily Feather / Danielle DiMartino Booth (QI Research)
items.title: Black Monday at 39: hyperscaler FCF has collapsed and IT hardware output fell in September
items.idea: Friday's Nasdaq 100 sell-off was 2.5%, 'an order of magnitude off' 1987, but QI flags that aggregate free cash flow across major hyperscalers has collapsed and could turn negative. Friday's Industrial Production showed IT hardware IP fell MoM in September, a month with no major AI-player bond issuances. The economy 'has all its eggs in the AI-buildout basket'.
items.angle: FCF to zero, no new bond issuance, hardware output falling: three independent tells that capex funding is the choke point.
items.tweetA: No AI bond deals in September and IT hardware output down. When the financing window closes before the capex does, something has to give. Watch the next hyperscaler issuance.
items.tweetB: Hyperscaler FCF heading to zero while capex guides up. Shareholder returns were the shock absorber. Now it's the balance sheet. $MSFT $AMZN $GOOGL $META

items.source: Early Morning with Dave / David Rosenberg
items.title: Rosenberg: bubbles deflate where the leverage is — CoreWeave, Oracle and SoftBank
items.idea: Rosenberg's key takeaway: the question is whether the AI boom is bursting at the core or cracking at the leveraged edge, which is where every credit-fueled bubble starts. The bond market is asking who pays for this and at what cost of capital. Named stress points: CoreWeave, Oracle, SoftBank. (Email shows only the first takeaway; full piece behind the link.)
items.angle: Third voice in this window (Goldman/Curtin, Boockvar) converging on financing cost as the AI trade's constraint.
items.tweetA: Equity says AI. Credit says who pays. Sooner or later one of them is wrong, and the credit market doesn't rally on narratives. $ORCL $CRWV
items.tweetB: Bubbles don't pop at the center, they pop at the most levered counterparty. Pick your candidate: $CRWV, $ORCL, SoftBank. I'd want spreads, not stock prices.

items.title: CoreWeave matters because data-center building drives the whole AI supply chain; IPOs at Firmus and AirTrunk cancelled, Nscale maybe
items.idea: Boockvar: CoreWeave's fate, and cancelled IPOs of Firmus and AirTrunk (maybe Nscale next), matter because data-center construction feeds semis, servers, transformers, electrical gear, HVAC, steel, cement, aluminum. Spend stays robust next year but stocks move on rate of change, so watch that over absolute capex. Rising financing costs raise questions about construction speed and US model quality vs China.
items.angle: Rate-of-change framing is the trade: second derivative of capex hits electrical/industrial names first.
items.tweetA: Nobody sells a transformer to a data center that can't raise money. Firmus, AirTrunk, maybe Nscale: three IPO windows shut in weeks. Second derivative is the trade.
items.tweetB: Capex at record levels and the stocks falling isn't a contradiction. It's what peak rate-of-change looks like. Ask where the ebitda of the electrical supply chain comes from in 2027.

items.title: France: CAC -1.4%, 10y OAT +9bp to 4.90%, euro weaker as unrest weighs
items.idea: Boockvar ties the CAC's 1.4% drop, a 9bp rise in the French 10y to 4.90% and a weaker euro to the political and social turmoil in France (rioting, property destruction). Mando Minutes separately notes 550k took to the streets.
items.angle: France is the sovereign Goldman flagged as vulnerable. Politics plus supply plus a 4.90% coupon is the setup for a spread event.
items.tweetA: 4.90% on the OAT with 550k in the streets. Fiscal credibility is a political variable now, and Bund-OAT is the instrument that trades it.
items.tweetB: Goldman says France is the cracking sovereign, Boockvar says OAT 4.90% on riots. That's two sources for one trade and the market is still treating it as a headline.

items.title: TIC: Japan sheds $35.6B of Treasuries to $1.068T, 4th straight monthly fall; China also paring
items.idea: August TIC: Japan, the largest foreign holder, cut holdings by $35.6B to $1.068T, near the lowest since 2019 and down 4 months in a row. China also continues to reduce. Boockvar notes some of this is mark-to-market, and asks at what JGB yield Japanese institutions repatriate.
items.angle: Marginal buyer question. Pair with Capital Wars' 'normal rates' piece: who funds $2T deficits when the two biggest holders net sell?
items.tweetA: Japan has sold Treasuries four months running. The largest foreign holder is now a net seller into a 10y that just broke out. Repatriation level on JGBs is the number I'm looking for.
items.tweetB: Japan's UST holdings are back near 2019 lows while its own yields rise. Every basis point JGBs add is a reason to bring money home. The bid under US duration has a Tokyo address.

items.title: Crypto weekly: BTC -1.4%, alts -7.5% average; top 12 losers -21.4%
items.idea: BTC $82,161 down 1.43% on week, +1% over 30 days. ETH -5.26%, SOL -6.54%, XRP -7.21%, DOGE -9.47%, HYPE -9.02%, ZEC -11.5%; average non-BTC major fall 7.5%, ~5x BTC. Starknet -45%, LayerZero -23%, Pump.fun -22%. 'Trenches index' hit 'cold' for the first time since April after euphoria in Aug–Sept.
items.angle: Classic dominance rotation (BTC.D 60.3% per Mando). Alt beta is being paid out only when BTC is sold. Trenches turning cold is a sentiment low marker.
items.tweetA: BTC lost 1.4% in a week. The average major lost 7.5%. That's not a crypto selloff, it's a liquidity haircut on everything that isn't bitcoin.
items.tweetB: Trenches index went cold for the first time since April. Euphoria in August, dead in October. Sentiment indicators are lagging, but it's usually the last one to flip.

items.title: ETH ETFs: $14.5B net assets vs $12.9B cumulative inflows — only $1.6B cushion before the product is underwater
items.idea: Spot BTC ETFs shed $228.4M and ETH ETFs $320.1M last week (combined $548.5M); October outflows now $1.86B. Ethereum ETF net assets of $14.5B against $12.9B cumulative net inflows leaves ~$1.6B of cushion before aggregate cost basis is underwater.
items.angle: Aggregate cost basis is a real support/risk level for flows. ETH ETF holders flip red around ~$2,150 by my arithmetic (2,415 × 12.9/14.5).
items.tweetA: ETH ETFs hold $14.5B against $12.9B of inflows. Rough math puts aggregate cost basis near $2,150 ETH. Below it every holder is red, and ETF holders aren't diamond hands.
items.tweetB: $1.86B out of ETFs in October and the price held. Either the sellers are done or the next leg is forced. I'd watch the weekly flow on a -10% ETH day.

items.title: Crypto has no circuit breakers: Kospi tripped one last week, bitcoin trades through everything
items.idea: Black Monday 1987 was automated selling feeding automated selling with no breakers. Equities have them now (Kospi tripped one last week), crypto has none and trades weekends, as seen in the Oct 10, 2025 liquidation cascade. Author's contrarian read: widely expected crashes rarely happen; the current setup is a slow bleed with a modest bid.
items.angle: The asymmetry is that crypto is the only market that can express a macro shock on a Sunday.
items.tweetA: Kospi tripped a circuit breaker last week. Bitcoin can't. If equities gap Monday, crypto already priced it Sunday night. That's a feature when you want to hedge.
items.tweetB: Everyone is quoting Black Monday calls. Everybody positioned for it is the reason it won't be the same shape. The real tail is the one nobody has a headline for.

items.title: Goldman, Wells Fargo, Morgan Stanley call tokenization an opportunity; Wells' tokenized-deposit payments already in production
items.idea: On Q3 calls all three banks framed tokenization as growth, not threat; Solomon compared it to electronic stock trading's rise. Wells Fargo said its tokenized-deposit payments system is live. Nine firms including Broadcom, Verizon, UnitedHealth have objected to trading on OKX-ICE's tokenized stock venue, an early test of the SEC's five-year Innovation Exemption.
items.angle: Incumbents embrace the rails; issuers resist the venue. That's the real split: infrastructure vs. price discovery of your own stock.
items.tweetA: Banks love tokenization when they run the rails. Issuers hate it when someone else trades their stock on them. The fight is over who owns the order book.
items.tweetB: Wells Fargo has tokenized deposits live in production. Not a pilot. Meanwhile nine issuers are opting out of tokenized stocks. Rails are won, venues are not.

items.title: Circle expands to ~40 emerging markets, says demand is organic across SE Asia, LatAm, Africa, Middle East
items.idea: Circle CEO Jeremy Allaire told the IMF/World Bank meetings in Bangkok that organic demand across SE Asia, LatAm, Africa and the Middle East is pulling stablecoins out of the early-adopter phase; Circle plans to expand into ~40 emerging countries.
items.angle: De-dollarization is the wrong frame; this is dollarization via API, which is the opposite.
items.tweetA: Allaire at the IMF: 40 emerging markets next. Every one of those users is a new holder of dollar liabilities with no Fed account. Stablecoins are the cheapest dollar distribution ever built. $CRCL
items.tweetB: Everyone says de-dollarization. Circle is shipping the opposite to 40 countries. Dollar share rises where banks fail users.

items.title: Circle: 59 cents of each revenue dollar goes to partners and transaction costs; net profit ~7 cents
items.idea: In H1 2026 about $819M of roughly $1.4B revenue went to USDC distribution partners and transaction costs, i.e. 59%. Circle kept ~7 cents of net profit per revenue dollar.
items.angle: Distribution owns the margin. Coinbase captures the yield; Circle is a float-management utility with a 41% gross take.
items.tweetA: 59 cents of every Circle revenue dollar goes to someone else. The issuer takes the regulatory risk and the distributor takes the economics. $CRCL $COIN
items.tweetB: Circle nets ~7% on revenue. Run that against a falling-rate scenario: revenue is a carry trade with a partner who takes more than half.

items.title: BIS paper: stablecoin growth slowed when bank deposit rates rose; USDC more exposed than USDT
items.idea: BIS working paper (Oct 13): across 339 weeks of US data, Jan 2019 to Jun 2025, stablecoin market value rose ~15% on average in a 10-week window. After a 1bp rise in deposit rates, baseline estimate falls to ~12% (second method ~6%). Effect larger for USDC than USDT. 'Growth slows but does not necessarily reverse'; sample covers one high-rate period.
items.angle: The first empirical evidence that stablecoins compete with deposits at the margin. Implication for GENIUS-style yield debates.
items.tweetA: BIS: stablecoins are a deposit substitute, and they behave like one. A 1bp rise in deposit rates cuts 10-week growth. USDC is more rate-sensitive than USDT, which tells you who holds which.
items.tweetB: The same stablecoin that will 'replace banks' slows down when banks pay a bit more. It's a money-market product with a tailwind in zero-rate years.

items.title: OKX-ICE tokenized-stock venue: nine objections incl. Broadcom, Verizon, CoreWeave, UnitedHealth
items.idea: Under the SEC exemptive order, one written objection in the 30-day notice window bars the venue from offering that stock. Notice went from 63 stocks and one objection (Cerebras) on Oct 4, to AppLovin, Applied Digital, Rocket Lab on Oct 8, to Broadcom, Verizon, UnitedHealth, CoreWeave, Applied Optoelectronics on Oct 15. Trading would run via permissioned Uniswap v4 pools on X Layer.
items.angle: The opt-out veto is the whole product risk. A venue where issuers can individually kill listings is structurally an opt-in market.
items.tweetA: The SEC gave issuers a veto. Nine of 63 used it in 11 days. If it trends to 20, the 'exemption' is a menu issuers can strike from.
items.tweetB: Companies don't want a fully crypto-native liquid market in their own stock. That tells you what the CFO thinks about the price signal. $AVGO $VZ $CRWV

items.title: Three exploits in a weekend: Qubic 1,404 wallets, Cysic 10M tokens minted, Ledger implant reports
items.idea: Qubic halted after an attacker drained 1,404 wallets via weak seeds. Cysic suspended its bridge after unauthorized minting of 10M CYS on BNB Chain and ~$727K moved to Ethereum. Mark Karpelès says Ledger spy implants turned up in devices from two more authorized resellers (Metapod Singapore, MediaMarkt Germany); Ledger says confirmed drains involve CryptoBilis devices and German retail stock showed no tampering.
items.angle: Supply-chain compromise in hardware wallets is a distinct risk class from smart-contract risk. Watch custody-vendor response.
items.tweetA: 1,404 wallets drained because of weak seeds. We build quantum-safe signatures while basic entropy fails. Security stack is only as strong as the RNG.
items.tweetB: Hardware wallet supply chain is now the attack surface. Resellers, not firmware. If you buy a Ledger from a third party, that's your threat model.

items.title: Brent at $108.47 after five-month high; BTC rises as oil pulls back
items.idea: Front-month Brent $108.47, down 1.3% from Friday's close which was the highest since May 19. Nasdaq 100 futures +1.1%, S&P +0.5%. BTC ~$83,007 (+1.1% 24h). Nexo analyst says reclaim of $84K plus a second day of ETF inflows would signal buyers returning, with $80K the level to hold. Note: Lucky Trader lists oil +4% at $101 in the same window — sources disagree on level.
items.angle: Oil above $100 plus bond yield breakout is the stagflation pairing. Verify the oil print before trading it.
items.tweetA: Brent at $108 and the Nasdaq futures are bid on a Putin summit headline. Oil is telling you the market doesn't believe the peace. $XLE
items.tweetB: Two sources, two Brent numbers: $101 and $108. The difference is the front-month roll. Check what you're actually comparing.

items.title: Tokenized stocks: Binance bStocks cross $1B AUM; Ondo $893.7M; Deutsche Bank crypto custody German launch weeks away
items.idea: Binance says bStocks crossed $1B AUM; rwa.xyz ranks it first at $1.2B vs Ondo's $893.7M. Deutsche Bank prepares German crypto custody launch in coming weeks (BTC, ETH, USDC, EURC, EURAU) with Asia expansion in 2027. World pitched banks a bundle of human-verification tools (World ID for Zoom now GA).
items.angle: Retail-facing tokenization is scaling faster than the exchange-listed version.
items.tweetA: Binance is the #1 tokenized stock platform at $1.2B. Wall Street's venue has nine issuers objecting. The disruption is happening where there's no issuer to ask permission.
items.tweetB: Deutsche Bank launching custody with EURAU and EURC listed. The euro stablecoin race is real and under-covered.

items.title: Missouri AG orders six companies to stop sports event contracts; Crypto.com and Novig sue
items.idea: Crypto.com and Novig sued Missouri in federal court after the state AG ordered six companies to stop offering sports event contracts. Kalshi, Polymarket, Robinhood and Underdog got the same letters but hadn't sued as of Sunday.
items.angle: State vs federal on prediction markets is heading to a circuit-split style outcome.
items.tweetA: Six companies, one state letter, two lawsuits. The prediction market fight is a state/federal preemption case, and it'll decide whether event contracts are derivatives or gambling.
items.tweetB: Kalshi and Polymarket haven't sued. That's either confidence or a different strategy. Watch which one.

items.title: Fairshake has spent ~$46.66M to keep Sherrod Brown out; judge refuses to let CFTC unwind its $5M Gemini settlement
items.idea: Crypto super PAC Fairshake has now spent about $46.66M against Sherrod Brown, plus a $5.2M media buy and a second $1.95M buy this month in Ohio. Separately a federal judge refused to let CFTC and Gemini vacate the 2025 consent order, saying shifting enforcement priorities and misconduct allegations don't undo a voluntary deal.
items.angle: Crypto's political spend is now at campaign-scale for a single seat. Court signal: enforcement retreat has legal limits.
items.tweetA: $46.66M to defeat one Senate candidate. For scale, that's more than most Senate races raise in total. The industry decided Brown is a regulatory risk.
items.tweetB: A judge told the CFTC it can't undo a settlement it signed just because priorities changed. Enforcement walk-backs have a court cost now.

items.title: Poor breadth: share of days with net new highs over new lows has collapsed over the past year
items.idea: Hi Mount tracks the spread of NYSE+NASDAQ new highs minus new lows. The percentage of days in the last year where highs exceeded lows has collapsed; when lows exceed highs, returns are more muted and volatility higher. Long-term trends haven't cracked, but 'more evidence of bear market behavior'. Their conclusion: capital preservation over chasing returns.
items.angle: Breadth says the index is the story and the average stock is already in a bear. That matches the hedge-fund hedging picture.
items.tweetA: The index is being held up by a few names while the majority print more new lows than highs. That isn't a correction, that's a rotation out of the average stock.
items.tweetB: When new lows beat new highs, volatility is elevated and returns muted. We have both. The 'buy the dip' base rate was built on broad markets.

items.title: Nominal wages and retail sales at highs, but flat in real terms for half a decade — plus a 10y breakout
items.idea: Average weekly earnings and retail sales hit new nominal highs but haven't grown in real terms over the past five years. The 10y yield broke out after years sideways to the highest in decades; debt service rises for the federal government, corporates and households. Core vs headline: food, restaurants and gas are the 'core' for consumers.
items.angle: Real income flat, debt service up. That's the consumer side of the Capital Wars 'normal rates' story.
items.tweetA: Nominal spending at all-time highs, real spending flat for five years. What you pay goes up, what you get stays the same. That's not a recovery.
items.tweetB: Economists defend 'ex food and energy'. Households pay for groceries and gas. Politicians know which one they're voting on.

items.title: Humanity's Last Exam: 8% in Jan 2025 to 67.7% now; FrontierMath 2% to 94%
items.idea: Clark's IMF (Bangkok, Oct 17) Per Jacobsson lecture: top AI score on Humanity's Last Exam went from 8% at launch (Jan 2025) to 67.7% this week (Claude Opus 5.5). FrontierMath, which launched in Nov 2024 with the best at 2%, is now at 94%. His claim: the singularity has begun. Disclosure: Clark co-founded Anthropic.
items.angle: Benchmark saturation in under two years. Treat the author's affiliation as a priors adjustment, but the numbers are the numbers.
items.tweetA: HLE: 8% to 67.7% in under two years. FrontierMath: 2% to 94%. Benchmarks designed to last a decade lasted eighteen months. The question isn't whether AI passes the test, it's who writes the next one.
items.tweetB: Author co-founded Anthropic, speaking at the IMF, saying the singularity has begun. Take the claim with a discount; keep the benchmark numbers at full price.

items.title: TheoPhysEval: AI scored 98% (49/50) after finding errors in the physicists' own answer keys
items.idea: Paper tests AI on 50 unpublished theoretical-physics problems written by physicists. Suvrat Raju: no individual can solve a significant fraction without AI. GPT-6-Astra initially scored late 80s, but insisted the expert answers were wrong; experts found subtle errors in their own calculations, and revised answers pushed Astra to 49/50.
items.angle: Evaluation breaks when the model is more reliable than the grader. That's an alignment and an accounting problem.
items.tweetA: The model argued with the answer key and won. When the test-setter is less reliable than the test-taker, you can't measure progress with human-written tests anymore.
items.tweetB: Physicists built a benchmark the model couldn't have seen, and the model corrected the benchmark. That's the part that should bother you.

items.title: Anthropic's own model: US GDP of $44T by 2030 under 'singularity' diffusion assumptions
items.idea: Clark cites internal Anthropic modeling: if models autonomously complete a broad range of tasks and diffuse quickly, US GDP could reach $44 trillion by 2030. He frames this as implying new industries must emerge. He also notes his researchers now write almost 10x the code of the company's first four years, and that UNESCO counts ~10M scientists globally versus potentially a billion virtual scientists.
items.angle: A scenario, not a forecast, from an interested party. Compare to current ~$30T and consensus real growth of ~2%: that's ~8%/yr compounding.
items.tweetA: $44T by 2030 implies roughly 8% annual growth from here. Consensus is 2%. Either the author is wrong or every long-duration asset is mispriced. I'd rather know which.
items.tweetB: 10 million human scientists today, a billion virtual ones in the model. If research labor gets 100x cheaper, the scarce input becomes labs and compute, not PhDs. $NVDA $TMO

items.title: Clark: data-center capacity concentrated in US, China, Middle East; next phase is robots and automated labs
items.idea: Clark says the first phase was compute and power, and few policymakers listened; capacity is now concentrated in the US, China and increasingly the Middle East, with supply chains contested enough that prices rise. The next phase is physical: AI operating robots and lab equipment, requiring more scientific equipment or capacity runs out. Developing countries supplying raw materials could leapfrog.
items.angle: The 'picks and shovels' sequel is lab automation and robotics supply chain.
items.tweetA: Phase one was compute. Phase two is atoms: robots, wet labs, materials testing. That's the next AI capex wave and it hasn't been priced.
items.tweetB: Anthropic's co-founder tells the IMF to build lab capacity before AI-designed drugs outrun clinical testing. The bottleneck moves from discovery to trials.

items.title: Chip stocks shed $2T in longest slide since 2008 — while SOXL logs record $6.1B weekly inflows
items.idea: Mando headlines: chip stocks have lost $2T in the longest slide since 2008, while SOXL (3x semis ETF) took record $6.1B weekly inflows. Stocks had the largest weekly slide since Apr 2025; US bank stocks posted six straight weekly losses; Nasdaq $26,140 (-2%).
items.angle: Record leveraged inflows into a falling sector is the positioning tell.
items.tweetA: Chips lost $2T. Retail put in a record $6.1B into 3x semis in the same week. That's not capitulation, that's the opposite.
items.tweetB: Longest semis slide since 2008 and the marginal buyer is a leveraged ETF. Who's on the other side of that trade by Friday?

items.title: Anthropic Q3 revenue reportedly +46% q/q to $16.8B; pays Blackstone 10%+ on $9B chip debt
items.idea: Reported (via X, unverified): Anthropic Q3 revenue up 46% q/q to $16.8B; separately it pays Blackstone 10%+ on $9B of chip-related debt. Also: NYC comptroller urges Anthropic to delay IPO; Anthropic puts at least 5% of shares in a public benefit fund; Musk says he would give Anthropic shares to public.
items.angle: Revenue growth with double-digit cost of debt on compute. The financing story from Goldman/Rosenberg, in one company.
items.tweetA: $16.8B in a quarter, up 46% q/q, and still paying 10%+ to finance chips. Hyper-growth doesn't buy you cheap capital when the asset is depreciating hardware.
items.tweetB: 46% q/q implies ~$11.5B last quarter. Annualized, that's over $65B. If it's real, the AI revenue skeptics have a very different denominator.

items.title: Neocloud shakeout looms; Microsoft pulls out of Nscale's UK data-center deal; CoreWeave on tokenization objection list
